subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 66-year-old man is evaluated for sudden weakness of the right arm and slurred speech that resolved within an hour. For the past 2 months he has had painless jaundice, dark urine, and a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss. CT shows a mass in the head of the pancreas. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a small, friable-appearing mass on the mitral valve leaflet. Three sets of blood cultures are negative.
question: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of the valvular lesion?

options.text: Bacterial colonization of a previously damaged valve leaflet
Immune complex deposition along the valve surface in the setting of autoantibodies
Sterile platelet-rich thrombus formation in the hypercoagulable state of advanced malignancy
Direct invasion of the valve annulus by pancreatic carcinoma cells
Chronic inflammation with fibrosis and calcification of the mitral valve leaflets

explanation_correct: This is nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis: sterile, platelet-rich vegetations that typically arise on the mitral or aortic valve and dislodge easily, so patients are usually asymptomatic until an embolic event such as a transient ischemic attack or stroke occurs. It is associated with the hypercoagulable state of advanced malignancy, especially pancreatic adenocarcinoma, which this patient's weight loss, painless jaundice, and pancreatic head mass indicate. Negative cultures distinguish it from infective endocarditis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Bacterial colonization of a damaged valve is the mechanism of subacute infective endocarditis, but three sets of negative cultures and the malignancy context point to a sterile, noninfective vegetation instead.
explanation_incorrect.B: Immune complex deposition along the valve is the mechanism of Libman-Sacks endocarditis in systemic lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune setting, not the paraneoplastic hypercoagulability described here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Marantic vegetations are sterile fibrin-platelet thrombi, not metastatic tumor deposits; pancreatic carcinoma embolizes or provokes thrombosis remotely rather than invading the valve annulus directly.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fibrosis and calcification of valve leaflets describe chronic degenerative or rheumatic valve disease, which produces stenosis rather than friable, easily dislodged vegetations with systemic emboli.

educationalObjective: Nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis consists of sterile platelet-rich vegetations on the mitral or aortic valve in hypercoagulable advanced malignancy, especially pancreatic adenocarcinoma, and usually presents with embolism.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for 2 weeks of fevers and malaise. She has a history of symmetric joint pain, a malar rash that worsens with sun exposure, and new-onset proteinuria. Temperature is 37.8°C (100.1°F). Transesophageal echocardiography shows small vegetations on both the atrial and ventricular surfaces of the mitral valve. Three sets of blood cultures are negative. Antinuclear and anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies are positive.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Marantic endocarditis associated with occult adenocarcinoma
Subacute infective endocarditis caused by viridans streptococci
Acute infective endocarditis caused by Staphylococcus aureus

explanation_correct: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis occurring in the setting of systemic lupus erythematosus is called Libman-Sacks endocarditis. The clue is the small, sterile vegetations on both surfaces of the mitral valve in a young woman with malar rash, photosensitivity, arthritis, proteinuria, and anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies. As in all nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, the vegetations are sterile (repeatedly negative cultures) and the patient may remain asymptomatic until embolism occurs.

explanation_incorrect.B: Marantic endocarditis is the same category of sterile vegetation, but the malignancy-associated form is linked to advanced cancer, especially pancreatic adenocarcinoma; this patient has classic SLE features and positive autoantibodies instead.
explanation_incorrect.C: Viridans streptococcal endocarditis requires positive blood cultures and typically follows dental procedures with larger vegetations on damaged valves; cultures here are repeatedly negative.
explanation_incorrect.D: Acute Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis produces large, destructive vegetations on previously normal valves with high fever and positive cultures, none of which are present, and vegetations on both valve surfaces are characteristic of Libman-Sacks disease.
explanation_incorrect.E: Rheumatic valvulitis follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis and presents with mitral regurgitation and Aschoff bodies in a younger patient with Jones criteria findings, not with bilateral valve-surface vegetations and lupus serologies.

educationalObjective: Libman-Sacks endocarditis is the form of nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis associated with systemic lupus erythematosus, featuring sterile vegetations on both sides of the mitral valve.
